extracted.intended_audience: AP teachers, AP exam readers, and students preparing for AP English Literature free-response essays
extracted.subtask_description: Scoring guidelines and sample commentary for AP English Literature and Composition Free-Response essays (poetry analysis, prose-fiction analysis, and literary argument). Explains point-by-point criteria (Thesis, Evidence & Commentary, Sophistication), examples, decision rules, and scoring notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis (Row A) — 0-1 points
rubrics_metrics.description: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the poem/passage/selected work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring Criteria: 0 points for any of the following: there is no defensible thesis; the intended thesis only restates the prompt; the intended thesis provides a summary with no coherent claim; there is a thesis but it does not respond to the prompt. 1 point: Responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the poem/passage/selected work. Responses that do not earn this point: only restate the prompt; make a generalized comment that doesn’t respond to the prompt; describe the poem or features rather than making a claim that requires defense. Examples that earn the point include explicit, defensible interpretive claims (sample phrasings provided in the guidelines). Decision Rules and Scoring Notes: The thesis may be more than one sentence and may be anywhere within the response. For a thesis to be defensible, the selected text must include at least minimal evidence that could be used to support the thesis; however, the student need not cite that evidence to earn the thesis point. A thesis that meets criteria can be awarded whether or not the rest of the response successfully supports that line of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence and Commentary (Row B) — 0-4 points
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and use evidence to support a line of reasoning and explain how the evidence supports that reasoning; combined scoring for EVIDENCE (0-4) and COMMENTARY (quality of explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring Criteria (EVIDENCE): 0 points — simply restates thesis, repeats provided information, or offers information irrelevant to the prompt. 1 point (Evidence): Provides evidence that is mostly general. 2 points (Evidence): Provides some specific, relevant evidence. 3 points (Evidence): Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. 4 points (Evidence): Provides specific evidence to support all claims in a line of reasoning. (COMMENTARY tiers aligned with evidence tiers): 0 — summarizes evidence but does not explain how the evidence supports the argument; 1 — summarizes evidence but does not explain how it supports the student's argument; 2 — explains how some evidence relates to the argument but no coherent line of reasoning is established or the line is faulty; 3 — explains how some of the evidence supports a line of reasoning and explains how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning; 4 — consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning and explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Typical response descriptions: 1-point responses tend to focus on summary/description rather than specific details or connect literary elements with little explanation; 2-point responses mix specific evidence and broad generalities and may lack progression; 3-point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims and focus on specific words/details but commentary may fail to integrate some evidence; 4-point responses uniformly offer evidence to support claims, organize an argument as a line of reasoning composed of multiple supporting claims with adequate evidence clearly explained. Additional Notes: Writing that suffers from grammatical and/or mechanical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the fourth point in this row. To earn the fourth point, a response may observe multiple instances of the same literary element if each instance further contributes to meaning. (Also: for the literary-argument prompt, to earn the fourth point the response must address the interpretation of the selected work as a whole.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Sophistication (Row C) — 0-1 points
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring Criteria: 0 points — does not meet criteria. 1 point — demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument. Responses that do not earn this point: attempts that consist predominantly of sweeping generalizations; only hinting at other interpretations; single thematic statements without sustained development; oversimplifying complexities; using complex language ineffectively. Responses that earn the point may do any of the following: identify and explore complexities or tensions within the text; account for alternative interpretations; illuminate the interpretation by situating it in a broader context; employ a style that is consistently vivid and persuasive. Additional Notes: The sophistication must be part of the student's argument (not merely a phrase or reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required response components / task instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit instructions given to students about what their essay must do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In your response you should do the following: Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation; Select and use evidence to support your line of reasoning; Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning; Use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument. These four bullets are both production requirements and the basis for scoring (they map to the rows above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time suggestion and weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested timing and score weighting for each free-response question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested time — 40 minutes for each of Questions 1 and 2 (as printed); each of these questions counts as one-third of the total essay section score. (This guidance informs student time allocation and the relative importance of each prompt.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rules, examples, and anti-patterns (scoring guidance and exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete examples, exemplar responses, and explicit anti-patterns used to illustrate scoring decisions across point levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidelines provide exemplars of responses that earn or do not earn specific points (sample thesis statements that fail because they restate the prompt; sample theses that earn the point because they provide defensible interpretations). They list typical features of responses at each score-level (e.g., 1-point responses focus on summary; 3-point responses focus on specific words and details; 4-point responses organize a line of reasoning composed of multiple supporting claims each with adequate evidence). Anti-patterns include: restating the prompt as thesis; merely describing the work or listing devices without connecting to argument; summarizing evidence without commentary; oversimplifying complexities; grammatical/mechanical errors that interfere with communication (precludes highest Evidence point). Scoring Notes also remind readers that the thesis point may be awarded even if the rest of the response fails to support it, and that the thesis may be located anywhere in the essay.
